questions.q: The retailers' inventory-to-sales ratio is called a lagging indicator because:
options: It measures demand, which always lags supply
It rises before a recession begins
It peaks only in the middle of a recession, after trouble has set in
questions.why: Stock visibly piles up only after demand has already fallen - the dial confirms the recession from inside it.

questions.q: The key operations difference between the 2008 and 2020 recessions was:
options: 2008 was demand-led with stable supply; in 2020 supply collapsed too and could not restart as fast as demand returned
questions.why: 2008: no demand for available supply. 2020: demand rebounded before supply was ready.

questions.q: China+1 - keeping China but adding a second manufacturing base in India or Vietnam - is an example of:
questions.why: De-risking = diversifying so no one geography holds you hostage; decoupling is rebuilding capability at home.

questions.q: The US semiconductor push (CHIPS Act) discovered that the real constraint on decoupling is:
questions.why: Money was never the bottleneck; decades of offshoring diluted the capability itself.

questions.q: Rare-earth metals give China leverage primarily because of its dominance in:
questions.why: Rare earths are not rare; the chokepoint is refining, which China dominates.

questions.q: IndiGo's decision to compete on low cost belongs to which level of the strategy cascade?
questions.why: Business strategy answers 'how to play' - the basis of competition. Entering aviation at all was corporate.

questions.q: The test of real differentiation, per the Harvard example, is:
options: What still stands once you strip away everything rivals can equally claim
questions.why: Harvard's answer is the case-study method - something rivals cannot equally say.

questions.q: Ford's 'any colour so long as it is black' is a deliberate position of:
options: Low variety, low cost via mass production
questions.why: Ford surrendered variety to win on cost - a captured trade-off.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the cost cascade unlocked by IndiGo's single fleet type?
options: Lower unit cost from large single-type orders
Premium pricing power on trunk routes
questions.why: The single fleet unlocks cost, not pricing power - IndiGo competes on price, not premiums.

questions.q: IndiGo's engine groundings show that standardisation's hidden price is:
options: Concentrated exposure when the one common component fails
questions.why: One dominant engine type means one fault hits the whole fleet - hence supplier-penalty revenue in its accounts.

questions.q: A firm sits below the industry benchmarking curve. The correct board reading is:
options: It chose too little value - raise the value target
It is the industry cost leader
It is operationally inefficient - the same value is achievable at lower cost
The curve does not apply to innovative industries
questions.why: The value level is the firm's prerogative; delivering it above frontier cost is the crime.

questions.q: In V = C x (A + P), the four questions carried by Assets are:
questions.why: Assets = sizing, timing, type, location; supply/technology/demand/innovation/risk sit under Processes.

questions.q: By producing in small lots, Zara deliberately trades:
questions.why: Small lots cut unsold-stock risk but invite stockouts - which Zara converts into scarcity marketing plus rapid replenishment.

questions.q: The deepest lesson of GM's 2009 bankruptcy despite a 15-year Toyota partnership is:
options: Culture is part of the process, and cannot be copied even from inside the same plant
Lean does not work outside Japan
questions.why: The machines and checklists transferred; the culture did not - Toyota struggles to export it even to itself.

questions.q: Per the first law of disruption, a disruptor must:
options: Kill an accepted trade-off, at scale
questions.why: Dell (variety at low cost) and Tesla (post-Gigafactory scale) both broke a trade-off at scale; niches are not disruptions.

questions.q: Apple is classified as product-innovation-led chiefly because:
options: Its manufacturing ecosystem is the industry's shared asset, not proprietary to Apple
questions.why: Foxconn's ecosystem serves many customers; Apple's edge rests on the next launch - the fragile side of the moat.

questions.q: Match the shock to its trigger, as taught in class:
options: Dot-com: political; 2008: biological; 2020: financial; tariffs: random natural events
Dot-com: tech bust (~2000); 2008: financial; 2020: biological; tariff era: political - and far more random than the others
questions.why: Each shock has a different trigger, but all landed first and hardest on operations - the function matching supply and demand.

questions.q: Why did supply recover so slowly in 2020, per the class?
options: Decades of globalisation chasing labour arbitrage built a deeply connected world - efficient, but the connectivity became a transmission line for the shock
questions.why: India absorbed services, China manufacturing; the same links that made chains cheap made them fragile.

questions.q: Wall Street's decades of applauding 'asset-light' balance sheets meant that when reshoring arrived, firms:
options: Had too much cash to deploy
Were asked to recreate capacity they no longer knew how to run - the bottleneck was capability, not cash
Could simply unplug supply chains from China and snap them into the US
questions.why: Supply chains are not Lego bricks; owning few factories for decades dilutes the very capabilities reshoring needs.

questions.q: Friend-shoring, as defined in class, is:
options: Bringing production all the way home
Building factories near the home market
Sourcing from politically friendly countries - India buying Russian oil was the class framing
questions.why: Reshoring = home; nearshoring = near the home market; friend-shoring = friendly geographies.

questions.q: NVIDIA being the most valuable firm on earth was cited to prove that:
options: Access to 2-3 nanometre chips is decisive - without them there is no modern AI, and that capability is a slow sequential climb no latecomer can leapfrog
Chip assembly is the highest-value stage
questions.why: The frontier capability, not the brand, is the moat - which is exactly why India's fab push cannot jump the queue.

questions.q: L&T's differentiation, per the class, is:
options: Complexity - infrastructure projects no rival will touch
questions.why: Differentiation is whatever would be missed if you vanished; for L&T that is the projects nobody else attempts.

questions.q: A pharma firm competing on SPEED of new-molecule launches must accept that:
options: Flexible, bring-any-science capacity sits partly idle - you buy agility with idle assets
Its lines must be rigidly specialised
questions.why: The cost player builds one rigid line per molecule; the speed player pays for flexibility with idleness.

questions.q: Tata's Jaguar plant at Solihull was retrofitted for flexibility because:
options: The strategy changed - stop putting all innovation into one product on one rigid platform
questions.why: Change the mandate above and the asset design below must change with it - the cascade in action.

questions.q: On fleet risk, the class distinguished:
options: A whole configuration (like the A321) failing is the rarest of rare; component failure - like the P&W engines - is the real, live risk
Configuration failure is common; component failure is rare
questions.why: Standardisation concentrates exposure at the component level - the exact failure IndiGo lived through.

questions.q: Even the industry's LOWEST-COST producer can sit below the benchmarking curve because:
options: The frontier is defined by what is technologically possible, not by what today's best player achieves
questions.why: Being today's best is not the same as being at the technological frontier - the subtlety he insisted on.

questions.q: The Gartner Supply Chain Top 25 was introduced WITH a caveat:
options: It is biased toward conventional distribution-heavy chains and under-weights pure services
It ranks only manufacturers by revenue
questions.why: Useful conversation starter, biased instrument - Schneider Electric, NVIDIA and Cisco topped the 2025 list.

questions.q: Zara keeping cloth un-dyed until the last moment (postponement) exists to:
options: Delay commitment until real demand information arrives - dye to whatever is selling
questions.why: Postponement converts forecasting risk into response speed - one of the levers serving the single objective: reduce lead time.

questions.q: 'Culture eats strategy for breakfast, lunch and dinner' was used in class to explain:
options: Why Toyota cannot fully replicate its own quality outside Japan - culture is part of the process
questions.why: Machines and suppliers transfer; the cultural ingredient of a process moat does not - which is also why rivals cannot copy it.

questions.q: THE TELL for which innovation type dominates: Dell and Zara are 'doing the same thing' because:
options: Both are vertically integrated in Spain
In both, the value you consume is a product, but the innovation that delivers it lives in the process
questions.why: Customised PC, fast fashion - the product is ordinary; the assembly model and supply chain are the moat.

questions.q: Apple's surging services revenue was read in class as:
options: An attempt to diversify away from a saturating hardware product - the curse of product-led advantage
questions.why: When advantage rests on the next launch, you hedge the launch - services is that hedge.

questions.q: Second-generation AirPods can be built in Vietnam but the third generation still needs China because:
options: The manufacturing ecosystem took forty years to build and is the industry's shared asset - depth cannot be relocated quickly
questions.why: Foxconn serves many customers; the ecosystem is world-class but not Apple's alone - and not portable on demand.

questions.q: By the 100-percent-valid test, manpower is a resource and not an input because:
options: After the transformation it is fully intact, while inputs no longer exist
It appears on the balance sheet
questions.why: Iron ore vanishes into pig iron; the worker and furnace remain - the vanishing test settles every debate.

questions.q: In the cash-flow reading of a process:
options: Inputs are inflows, outputs are outflows
Inputs and resources are outflows; outputs are inflows
questions.why: A resource's outflow may be years old (depreciation), but it is an outflow all the same.

questions.q: The course definition of efficiency is:
options: For a given unit of output, minimising the inputs and resources required, in currency terms
Doing the right things for all stakeholders
questions.why: Efficiency is cost minimisation in polite clothing - the operational route to profit maximisation.

questions.q: Patancheru's antibiotic-resistance story illustrates that:
options: Aggressive efficiency relocates costs onto stakeholders outside your P&L
Regulation has no role in operations
questions.why: The saving showed as efficiency on the plant dashboard; the bill moved to the community's health.

questions.q: Effectiveness is defined in this course as maximising the welfare of:
questions.why: Efficiency already serves the shareholder; effectiveness need not repeat the favour.

questions.q: Customer welfare, precisely, equals:
questions.why: The Rs. 20 bottle worth Rs. 40 on a hot day gives Rs. 20 of welfare; on a rainy day, none - the value moved.

questions.q: Income-tax e-filing was classified as:
options: Both - department cost fell from ~Rs. 3 to ~Rs. 0.5 per Rs. 100 collected while citizen filing collapsed to minutes
questions.why: One redesign served the owner (cost) and the stakeholder (time) simultaneously.

questions.q: Zara is MORE profitable than efficient rivals despite 15-20% costlier materials because:
options: Its revenue quality is higher - customers hunt novelty and scarcity, and nobody asks for a discount
questions.why: Higher costs, higher-quality revenue, better margins - effectiveness producing efficiency's prize.

questions.q: The Lemon Tree mechanism, articulated in hindsight, is:
options: Disability hiring qualifies for tax breaks
A firm that visibly cares for its own people signals to guests that it will care for them
questions.why: Care is read by customers as reliability - the 'extra' cost became extra revenue.

questions.q: A layoff announcement lifting a share price is best described as:
options: Efficiency as theatre - the market applauds the cost signal before any cost is saved
questions.why: The signal, not the saving, moves the price - the opposite of the Lemon Tree design.

questions.q: The single point of betrayal in the old MDP process was:
options: Confirming every nomination instantly, then cancelling under-subscribed programmes after participants had booked travel
questions.why: Sequencing, not paperwork, was the killer: faculty viability now precedes any participant confirmation.

questions.q: A hospital doing one hundred identical cataract surgeries a day is best classified as:
questions.why: Repetitive, near-identical processing is an assembly line - and quality is the product of that process, not its casualty.

questions.q: Collate (2 min) then staple (1 min), one person each. Cycle time, throughput time and hourly output are:
questions.why: The slowest stage (collation) sets CT = 2; TP = 2 + 1 = 3; output = 60/2 = 30, while the stapler idles half the time.

questions.q: An aircraft's 30-40 minutes at the gate (deplaning, cleaning, boarding) is:
questions.why: It is preparation for the next flight - like scrubbing the kadai between dishes. The runway queue is the waiting time.

questions.q: An OPD has a 1-minute cycle time and a 1-hour visit. Average patients inside the system:
questions.why: Little's Law: WIP = throughput time x rate = 1 hour x 60/hour = 60.

questions.q: Dumper problem (load 7.5, round trip 25.5, shovel Rs. 200/hr, dumper Rs. 800/hr): to minimise cost per load, hire:
questions.why: Crossover n* = 25.5/7.5 = 3.4; three dumpers minimise cost per load, four merely finish fastest.

questions.q: In the departure terminal, the bottleneck and system capacity are:
questions.why: Check-in: 5 counters x 15/hour = 75, the lowest stage capacity - the system's capacity.

questions.q: To lift that terminal to 120 passengers/hour you must:
options: Add 3 check-in counters and 1 security counter
questions.why: Check-in needs 120/15 = 8 counters (+3); security 120/30 = 4 (+1); the other stages already stand at 120.

questions.q: Negative electricity prices - buyers paid to consume - were cited to show:
options: Even the cleanest mapping (outputs = inflows) has exceptions when supply swamps demand
Outputs are always cash inflows, no exceptions
questions.why: Rare, but a useful reminder: in spot markets, oversupply can flip the sign of the inflow.

questions.q: Standing in Calcutta while needing to be in Delhi is, in the transformation lens:
options: An input - an unmet need qualifies; you rent the airline's resources to transform it
questions.why: Inputs need not be physical; if we could all fly, airlines would have nothing to transform.

questions.q: Why does the word 'efficiency' survive in boardrooms while 'cost minimisation' draws resentment?
options: Only 'efficiency' passes as pure virtue - nobody hears their own job inside it
questions.why: Test the three phrases: profit maximisation and cost minimisation sound like someone pays; efficiency sounds like everyone wins.

questions.q: Sumit finishes in one hour what takes Biju three. Sumit's reward is:
options: The next task - same salary, more output; the employer's resource cost per unit falls
questions.why: That is exactly why it counts as efficiency: a paid resource's time per unit of output was minimised.

questions.q: The professor's cheeky 'peace formula' for employees ground down by efficiency drives:
options: Buy the company's shares - when the squeezing is high, the profits usually are too
questions.why: He held his old employer's stock for decades - partly nostalgia, mostly returns.

questions.q: His Rs. 50,000 Google Pixel, privately valued above Rs. 60,000, illustrates:
options: Welfare = value minus price: a surplus of Rs. 10,000-plus - and a sheepish thank-you to his son
questions.why: You buy when your value exceeds the price; the gap is your welfare.

questions.q: An employee valuing the job at Rs. 3 lakh while paid Rs. 2 lakh praises the firm - until a Rs. 2.5 lakh offer arrives. Lesson:
options: Employee welfare is the perceived value-minus-price gap, not the evening chocolates
questions.why: Shrink the surplus below an outside option and twenty years of loyalty evaporates by lunchtime.

questions.q: Selling only a single large pack size was classified as:
options: Efficiency - it favours the producer's cost structure, not the customer's actual need
questions.why: Flip it - smaller packs, more often - and the same product line moves toward effectiveness.

questions.q: One 100-seater bus every 30 minutes versus 25-seaters every 15 minutes:
options: The first is efficiency (producer's cost per seat); the flip to smaller-more-frequent is effectiveness
questions.why: Same route, same total seats - the design choice decides whose welfare is being optimised.

questions.q: 'Design', in the effectiveness discussion, means:
options: Every stakeholder considered in every decision - the women-workforce safe commute is part of the plant's design, not the government's headache
questions.why: A design that optimises for a subset of stakeholders is an incomplete design.

questions.q: Toyota spending 'extra' on employee and customer welfare is defended because:
options: An extra cost of 10 that returns more than 10 is not a cost at all
questions.why: It wants the best employees and best customers - effectiveness quietly producing efficiency's prize.

questions.q: The class evidence for process maps included all of these EXCEPT:
options: Maps eliminating the need for any digitisation
Swim lanes ending months of cross-functional blame
ISO and SOC audits being documented process at bottom
An Oracle-to-SAP migration where the maps WERE the migration
questions.why: Maps enable migration, accountability and audit; the MDP story still needed its Rs. 1.5 lakh portal.

questions.q: The professor's two-hospitals story (his cataract vs his mother-in-law's) teaches:
options: Reputation is not process - the small hospital ran like clockwork with a printed step-sheet; the reputed one ran on 'wait, we will tell you'
questions.why: He still wonders how the second place became the famous one.

questions.q: The MDP data upended intuition on programme length:
options: 5-6 day programmes ran 100% of the time; every 2-day was cancelled and more than half the 3-day ones died
questions.why: He had assumed busy executives prefer short programmes; the data said the opposite - and higher price filled MORE reliably ('a strange industry').

questions.q: The MDP repair cost about Rs. 1.5 lakh because:
options: The institute helped build the front end and the professor coded the back end himself - formal procurement would have taken a year or two
questions.why: Sequencing + communication + digitisation - not budget, not headcount - bought ~44% growth a year.

questions.q: The professor's half-joking weekly prescription:
options: Swap an hour of Netflix for an hour of process-wandering - 'is there some other way to do this?'
questions.why: The day job is boring; process change is where the creativity lives - and how careers get made.

questions.q: If cataract procedures hypothetically differed for men and women, the hospital would run women's and men's batches with a changeover - because:
options: The moment resource-sharing forces changeovers between dissimilar lots, you are batching
questions.why: That is the precise trigger separating a batch shop from a pure assembly line.

questions.q: His 4:30 am airport ride takes 45 minutes; the 4:30 pm ride takes two hours plus. The extra time decomposes into:
options: Operation plus waiting - plus even a mid-ride switch of cabs, which is a setup inside the journey
questions.why: Throughput time = setup + operation + waiting; the clock does not care which one is eating you.

questions.q: Rain cutting an intersection from 100 to 80 vehicles a minute can freeze a corridor because:
options: Little's Law: with arrivals steady, a lower throughput rate makes the accumulating queue explode - the maths, not the traffic police, is the villain
questions.why: One centimetre of rain can cripple Delhi or Bengaluru - queueing arithmetic at city scale.

questions.q: Takt time (from the after-class exchange) is:
options: The conveyor's pace that each station's cycle time must match - aligning the two is line balancing
questions.why: Car-industry vocabulary; his reading tip for that world was Arthur Hailey's novel Wheels.

questions.q: With four dumpers, each returning dumper waits 4.5 minutes while the fourth loads. The measures read:
options: Shovel 100%, dumpers 85% - capacity 8 loads/hour, the fastest but not the cheapest configuration
questions.why: Four maximises capacity (finish earliest); three minimises cost per load - the objectives disagree, which is the point.

questions.q: Istanbul airport's walk-through security (nothing removed, no belts, no laptops out) shows:
options: The deepest capacity lever is often process redesign - roughly doubling a lane's capacity without adding a counter
More counters is the only lever
questions.why: Before buying capacity, redesign the work the capacity does.

questions.q: The Zudio numbers that floored the professor:
options: Roughly a 47-day inventory cover, barely any discounting, a fortnight's end-of-season sale - at a Rs. 1,500 price point far below Zara's
questions.why: Not a copy-paste of Zara's economics, yet the fingerprints of small lots and frequent replenishment everywhere - with the chain kept deliberately opaque.

questions.q: The professor's estimate of how much of what we consume is make-to-stock:
questions.why: The MTO revolution never came; if anything, old MTO (uniform tailoring) migrated to MTS.

questions.q: Total source-to-consumption lead time is usually longer in MTS because:
options: The product is made months ahead and sleeps in warehouses en route
questions.why: The June packet of chips was made in April. What MTS compresses is the customer's order-to-delivery clock.

questions.q: The DEEP reason the make-to-order revolution never arrived:
options: Capital demands utilisation, and MTO structurally cannot run near 100% without endless queues
questions.why: MTS runs hot against a forecast; MTO running hot makes customers wait forever.

questions.q: Quick commerce's 15-minute promise is paid for by:
options: Deliberately low utilisation - idle riders and dark-store slack
questions.why: Staff a dark store to average demand and the promise dies the same day - you consume low utilisation as a service.

questions.q: Asian Paints' base-plus-tint model places the customisation boundary:
questions.why: Dell held the boundary at the factory; Asian Paints pushes it all the way to the dealer.

questions.q: Quick commerce, classified correctly, is:
questions.why: Limited variety held near you, behind a ten-minute thrill - all of MTS's constraints intact.

questions.q: In ABC analysis, A items are approximately:
questions.why: CV = annual demand x unit cost; Pareto's shape appears every time.

questions.q: The correct ordering-and-safety-stock policy for A items:
options: Small frequent lots, MORE days of safety stock
Big infrequent lots, more safety stock
Big infrequent lots, minimal safety stock
Small frequent lots, minimal safety stock
questions.why: Lot size follows holding cost (small); safety stock follows supply risk (high - few irreplaceable suppliers).

questions.q: A car chip - low value, but able to halt the industry - is, in the Kraljic view:
questions.why: Low value crossed with high supply risk = bottleneck; crude oil (high value, high risk) is strategic.

questions.q: Shortage cost is best described as:
options: Lost profit - revenue that never arrived, invisible in the accounts
questions.why: It looks like a cost but no dashboard shows it - which is why efficiency metrics under-weigh it.

questions.q: The two (and only two) inventory trade-offs are resolved by:
options: Ordering vs shortage and holding vs quality
Cyclic stock (ordering vs holding) and safety stock (holding vs shortage)
questions.why: There is no meaningful ordering-shortage trade-off; any inventory decomposes into Q/2 plus safety stock.

questions.q: D = 12,000/yr, S = Rs. 120/order, C = Rs. 10, I = 0.2. The EOQ is:
questions.why: H = I x C = 2; Q* = sqrt(2 x 12,000 x 120 / 2) = sqrt(1,440,000) = 1,200 - ten orders a year.

questions.q: At the EOQ, which relationship always holds?
options: Annual ordering cost equals annual holding cost
Ordering cost is double holding cost
questions.why: The U-curve's minimum sits exactly where the two annual costs cross.

questions.q: Dell declaring a 30% holding rate (vs the ~20% thumb rule) was:
options: Deliberate: a bigger H drives Q down, pushing Dell into tiny lots, JIT and its made-to-order machine
questions.why: One parameter, chosen with intent, became a business model.

questions.q: You order once every 30 days. Your cyclic stock, in days of demand:
questions.why: Cyclic stock = Q/2. If average inventory is 25 days and Q/2 is 15, safety stock = 10 days.

questions.q: Newsvendor: profit Rs. 7.5 per unit sold, Rs. 2.5 loss per leftover. The critical ratio is:
questions.why: CR = Cu/(Cu+Co) = 7.5/10 = 0.75 - pick the smallest Q whose cumulative probability reaches it.

questions.q: With cumulative probabilities 0.6 at 50, 0.7 at 60 and 0.8 at 70, the optimal stock at CR = 0.75 is:
questions.why: First cumulative at or above 0.75 is 0.8, at Q = 70 - matching the grid's Rs. 295 optimum.

questions.q: Service level, precisely, is:
options: The proportion of periods in which demand is met in full
questions.why: It is the cumulative probability you chose to satisfy - the newsvendor's dial.

questions.q: The Chingrighata Saturday (one crossing shut, every 10km-plus journey an hour late) opened the session to prove:
options: Operations theory has sat in textbooks for fifty-plus years, yet its usage - in firms and in cities - is still this thin
questions.why: He nearly retired this lecture as too obvious around 2013-14; then Amazon's rise put cycle time back into boardrooms.

questions.q: From the mid-1980s, operations 'fell out of several American MBA syllabi' because:
options: The narrative was captured by marketing, strategy (Porter, BCG) and finance - until Walmart, Dell and Amazon dragged it back
questions.why: 'Luckily, that did not happen in India' - and the firms that won the next decades won on operations.

questions.q: Match the MAIN operations problems to the system:
options: MTS: forecasting, production planning and inventory control; MTO: delivery promises and delivery time
questions.why: MTS fights uncertainty before demand arrives; MTO fights the clock after it does.

questions.q: The professor's childhood school uniform - designated-shop fabric, then a tailor sitting on it for a month - captured:
options: Both in one purchase: make-to-stock fabric feeding a make-to-order tailor
questions.why: And that old MTO tailoring has since migrated to MTS readymades - the opposite of the 1990s prophecy.

questions.q: Which lead-time clock does the CUSTOMER feel in full under MTO?
options: Order-to-delivery - the clock starts only when you order, and it is almost all processing
questions.why: MTS total lead time is longer (your June chips were made in April), but the customer-facing clock is short because stock sits nearby.

questions.q: Why can a pure MTO system never satisfy capital's demand for utilisation?
options: Run MTO near 100% and customers queue forever - the busy-ness capital demands is structurally incompatible with responsiveness
questions.why: MTS runs near 100% against a forecast; MTO must hold idle capacity to promise speed.

questions.q: Southwest squeezing 13-14 flying hours from an 18-hour day with 20-minute turnarounds is:
options: A standardised, MTS-style service chasing utilisation - the counter-current that proves the rule, not customisation
questions.why: Utilisation obsession works when the service is standardised; it kills you when the promise is responsiveness.

questions.q: Ferrari, Rolls-Royce and Rolex survive as pure MTO because they are:
options: Profitable value-over-volume niches - which is exactly what disruption is NOT
questions.why: A niche customising for the wealthy few existed a century ago; scale is what separates a niche from a disruption.

questions.q: The ATO scorecard from the slide reads:
options: Less inventory and faster service than pure MTO, at the price of some work-in-process inventory
More inventory and slower than MTO
questions.why: Measures that matter: speed of service, inventory levels, quality - and the design question is where the boundary sits.

questions.q: The professor mourned Big Basket's old hub-and-spoke model because dark stores mean:
options: Variety is shrinking - a store close to you holds only so many items; you buy 500g of bhindi because that is the pack
questions.why: His single weekly one-store trip has splintered into five or six app orders because no single app stocks everything.

questions.q: Match the Kraljic quadrants:
options: Bottleneck = low value but high supply risk; strategic = high value, high risk (crude oil); leverage = high value, low risk; the rest are non-critical
questions.why: ABC is the vanilla cut by value; Kraljic crosses value with supply risk - the chip that halts a car plant is a bottleneck item.

questions.q: 'COVID's chip crunch has become AI's' was the warning that:
options: Which item wears which label keeps rotating; no formula rescues you - this is where managers become stars or failures (beware hindsight)
questions.why: Every bold inventory call looks like grand strategy only after it pays.

questions.q: Open a manufacturer's P&L: where is 'inventory cost'?
options: In the COGS line as a true cost
Nowhere - it arrives in disguises (interest, rent, preservation, security, handling, depreciation): 'like Vishnu, inventory has many incarnations'
questions.why: COGS (opening + purchases - closing) is a flow computation, not the carrying cost - which is why silo owners each optimise a sliver.

questions.q: Which is NOT an assumption of the basic EOQ model?
questions.why: Uncertainty is precisely the NEXT model's job (the newsvendor); EOQ lives in the textbook world of constants.

questions.q: The newsvendor's interior optimum at 70 exists because:
options: Expected sales climb at a DECREASING rate while leftovers climb at an INCREASING rate - the good news flattens exactly as the bad news steepens
questions.why: Peak at 70, falling away on both sides - too much cushion is as costly as too little.

questions.q: The safety stock hiding inside the newsvendor solution (expected sales 47 at Q*=70):
questions.why: Starting stock minus expected sales - the cushion the critical ratio decided you should pay for.

questions.q: Milk and bread are 'India's best-run supply chains' because:
options: Perishability forced mastery - near-zero stockouts, nothing stale sold, almost nothing thrown away; chains without that whip tolerate sloppiness
questions.why: In twenty-plus years he has almost never faced a stockout - the newsvendor clock, mastered.

questions.q: Aged whisky is worth holding only while:
options: Each year's price appreciation beats that year's carrying cost - sell the moment it does not
questions.why: The mirror image of perishability - and on gold as an investment he remains a confessed sceptic.

questions.q: Once an engine sits inside a finished car, asking 'how many engines do you hold?' counts:
options: Only the loose ones - the fitted engine's identity is absorbed into car inventory (raw material, WIP, finished goods)
questions.why: Inventory changes form as it flows - exactly as the accounting sessions taught.

questions.q: Deciding how many fulfilment centres to build is OS; deciding this week's ordering quantities is OM. The distinction is:
options: OS designs the system (infrequent, capex-heavy, hard to reverse); OM runs it (continuous, correctable)
questions.why: 'Doing smart things' vs 'doing things smartly' - Intel executed OM brilliantly while its OS failed.

questions.q: In the semiconductor value chain, TSMC dominates:
questions.why: Design is Nvidia/AMD/Qualcomm; fabrication is TSMC (enabled by ASML's lithography monopoly); assembly is China/Korea/Japan.

questions.q: Intel's core error was:
options: Vertical integration in an industry whose next source of value creation had moved outside firm boundaries
questions.why: A control-first OS in a deliberately dis-integrated ecosystem - outsourcing there was the innovation engine.

questions.q: On the 787, Boeing's outsourcing share and supplier structure were approximately:
options: 70% with about 50 tier-1 partners and no visibility beyond tier 1
questions.why: Versus the 737's 35-50% and thousands of directly managed suppliers building to Boeing's designs.

questions.q: The risk-sharing contract (paid only when the airline pays Boeing) backfired in 2008 because:
options: Rational suppliers slowed down - why deliver early and lock working capital waiting for the slowest partner?
questions.why: A contract designed as a speed race became a slow race - model the incentives, not the intent.

questions.q: 'Traveled work' at Boeing refers to:
options: Jobs done out of sequence - unfinished planes pushed down the line, now 30-40% rework
questions.why: It is a culture metric wearing an operations costume.

questions.q: The correct verdict on vertical integration, per the Intel-Zara contrast:
options: Context decides: it buys CONTROL - right when your differentiator needs control (Zara's speed), wrong when value creation moved outside (Intel)
questions.why: Same tool, opposite verdicts - never answer good or bad without naming the basis of competition.

questions.q: The CAUSE (not symptom) of DMart's flywheel is:
options: A curated assortment of fast movers - low variability that makes low inventory possible
questions.why: Fast payment, liquidity and discounts are downstream; remove the curation and the flywheel stops.

questions.q: What actually drives safety stock levels?
options: Demand variability (noise) and the promised service level
questions.why: Predictable high volume needs near-zero buffer; erratic low volume can need plenty - a common mistake.

questions.q: A firm offering huge variety on a rigid, standardised process sits:
options: Below the diagonal - writing cheques its process cannot cash
Above the diagonal - paying for unused flexibility
questions.why: High variety on low flexibility means infeasible promises and heavy opportunity costs.

questions.q: Dell's position on the product-process matrix is:
options: ON the diagonal - mass-producing the standard 70-80% and customising only the final slice
questions.why: Calling Dell rigid disserves its variety; calling it fully flexible disserves its cost - its genius is staying on the line.

questions.q: Two plants (capacity 100 each) serve demands of 110 and 90. Dedicated vs flexible sales:
questions.why: Dedicated: 100 + 90 = 190 with stranded capacity; full flexibility serves all 200 - what the cross-links buy.

questions.q: SDN = 3, SDS = 4. Pooled SD at r = 0 and at r = -1:
questions.why: sqrt(9+16) = 5 at independence; sqrt(9+16-24) = 1 at perfect hedge; at r = +1 it is 7 - never worse than the sum.

questions.q: The one trade-off you must ALWAYS name alongside pooling's inventory saving:
options: Longer lead time - the pooled stock sits farther from the customer
questions.why: It is why Amazon runs regional centres and quick commerce runs dark stores, not one national mega-hub.

questions.q: When comparing two firms' sourcing choices, judge:
options: The fit between WHAT is outsourced and the order winner (innovation, quality, speed, cost)
questions.why: The Intel-Boeing-Zara triangle in one line.

questions.q: Hyperscaler data-centre counts, Nvidia's GPU commitments and Amazon's fulfilment square footage are all:
options: Live OS questions - sizing, timing, type and location of resources
questions.why: Capacity means different things per industry, but the resource questions are the OS core everywhere.

questions.q: The semiconductor industry deliberately dis-integrated because:
options: No single firm could fund every layer at innovation speed - specialised giants at each stage cross-pollinated (ASML made TSMC possible; TSMC made Nvidia feasible)
questions.why: Outsourcing here was never a cost trick; it was the industry's innovation engine - the fact Intel misread.

questions.q: ASML matters to the chip story because it is:
options: Europe's most valuable firm and the only maker of the lithography machines cutting-edge fabs need
questions.why: A one-firm chokepoint enabling stage 2 - which is why export controls target its machines.

questions.q: The Andy Grove irony:
options: Intel's most celebrated CEO literally wrote 'Only the Paranoid Survive' - and Intel then performed the innovator's dilemma it preached against
questions.why: Giants stop seeing innovation outside their walls - Intel taught the lesson twice, once in print and once in person.

questions.q: The Economist's 'curse of the top dog' data shows the most valuable S&P 500 firm:
options: Massively outperforms BEFORE reaching the top and underperforms the index AFTER
Keeps outperforming after reaching the top
questions.why: Google's TPU response - refusing to accept Nvidia dependence - is the counter-example of a giant that kept looking outside.

questions.q: Three Intel CEO changes in roughly three years (Gelsinger arrived in 2021 and was out by December 2024) show:
options: Capacity decisions are OS decisions, and OS mistakes cannot be fixed in a quarter
questions.why: The scoreboard row Boeing shares: 3 CEOs in about 3 years - both firms paying for decade-old design calls.

questions.q: The 787 was 'genuinely aspirational' because:
options: It promised the once-in-two-decades fuel-efficiency leap - which is why Air India ordered early and the Tata fleet is 787-heavy
questions.why: Five years late, then the first fleet-wide grounding of a jet type since 1979 - aspiration executed through a broken chain.

questions.q: 'A cost culture in a quality industry' refers to:
options: A finance-first board approving the Dreamliner chain only as a massively cost-controlled model - in an industry whose currency is quality
questions.why: The deeper disease that deserves no hindsight-mercy; the culture drifted from ingenuity and quality to shareholder returns.

questions.q: The corporate-politics coda of the Dreamliner design:
options: The executive who designed the chain lost the CEO race and went on to run Ford; the finance-minded board member who demanded the cost model became CEO
questions.why: Incentives and careers shaped the chain as much as engineering did.

questions.q: Boeing slicing itself into separate verticals - even separate headquarters - was done partly to:
options: Break unions and squeeze cost - destroying the intimacy between design and making that an aircraft demands
questions.why: Two decades of silos, then a new CEO finding 'about 30 percent of everybody's job is fixing something'.

questions.q: Tesla handing China its EV playbook via the Shanghai Gigafactory was:
options: A calculated trade-off: without China's scale, Tesla never escapes overpromise-and-underdeliver - and the same soil grew BYD
questions.why: Calibrated outsourcing: define what is core (it never leaves the building) and pay knowingly for the rest.

questions.q: The printed circuit board was pioneered by a contract manufacturer because:
options: Only a firm aggregating everyone's volumes had the scale to fund it - outsourcing as an R&D engine, the TSMC story two decades early
questions.why: At scale, the outsourcer can out-innovate any single customer - Samsung even earned more from Apple components than its own handsets at one point.

questions.q: Toyota's EV conservatism (world-class hybrids, slow on pure EVs) is now read as:
options: Vindicated - rival CEOs publicly conceded Toyota read it right; EV softness is demand risk, not dead capacity, and being smartly late is also an operations strategy
questions.why: Mocked for years, last laugh delivered - the sizing-and-timing boxes of V = C x (A+P) in action.

questions.q: Variance squares deviations because:
options: Overshoots and undershoots must not cancel (both are bad) and large misses deserve disproportionate punishment
questions.why: The square root - standard deviation - is the noise; in finance the same quantity wears a suit and is called volatility.

questions.q: Asked to analyse SpaceX, Uniqlo or 'my company', the professor's consistent answer was:
options: No standard script and no classroom consulting - take the first principles and do the heavy lifting on your own context
questions.why: 'You are here at IIM Calcutta to learn to ask questions, not to solve questions.'

questions.q: Apple's inventory turns (~70) vs Samsung's (~20) primarily reflect:
options: Different business models - narrow curated range vs every-price-point variety
questions.why: Operations KPIs are strategy readouts; benchmarking across different diagonals is meaningless.

questions.q: When Amazon densifies its warehouse network (un-pooling), which cost FALLS?
questions.why: Inventory and inbound rise (correlation benefit surrendered, more supplier links); only outbound falls - the parcel starts closer.

questions.q: Amazon's fulfilment cost percentage bending UP with scale is:
options: A conscious trade - speed-driven sales growth dominates the cost growth
A drift it failed to notice
questions.why: Un-pooling is only a mistake when it is a drift instead of a decision.

questions.q: A hub-and-spoke airline network is, in pooling terms:
options: Pooled - one consolidated node serving many spokes
questions.why: Hubs pool crew, aircraft and slack; point-to-point keeps city pairs independent.

questions.q: Southwest's December 2022 meltdown (16,000+ cancellations, months to recover) happened because:
options: A system-wide storm demanded reallocation, and its point-to-point design had no pooled slack to reallocate
questions.why: Hub carriers re-pooled their way out in days. Every design chooses which disaster it cannot absorb.

questions.q: The FAIR criticism of IndiGo's December 2025 is:
options: Management injected a fully plannable (deterministic) rostering change at short notice into a zero-slack system
It should carry spare aircraft everywhere
questions.why: Weather is not their fault; a self-inflicted shock into a system with no absorbers is.

questions.q: Netflix's REAL disruption was:
options: DVD-by-mail on ~50 pooled warehouses - unlimited variety at low cost, killing a trade-off
questions.why: OTT was a progression it surfed; the moat was the subscriber base the pooled mail model built.

questions.q: The revenue-sharing contract fixed DVD rental's broken economics by:
options: Cutting wholesale to ~USD 10 and sharing roughly half of every rental with the distributor
questions.why: High wholesale plus uncertain demand caused under-ordering; sharing the upside made retailers stock fully.

questions.q: FedEx merged Ground and Express because B2B and B2C demand streams had turned:
questions.why: One shrank as the other exploded; pooling is exactly the shock absorber for negatively correlated streams.

questions.q: The 2020s' entry on the hundred-year variable-cost ladder is:
options: Cognition itself - agents billed per token, per task
questions.why: Taylor made output variable, the 90s labour, the 2000s services; agentic AI prices thinking.

questions.q: Jevons paradox, token edition, warns that:
options: As unit cost falls, use cases and agentic depth multiply - budget for C x N, not C
Cheaper tokens shrink the AI bill
questions.why: Klarna wins at shallow depth (~USD 0.19/resolution); the Microsoft-Uber zone lies past the crossover.

questions.q: Per the module, the correct stance on agentic AI is:
options: Outsource tasks; never transfer capabilities - recovery cost can be infinite
questions.why: The Boeing-Spirit mistake at organisational scale: once the team is gone, nobody is left to redesign.

questions.q: The andon cord's real function at Toyota is:
options: Surfacing quality problems - anyone can stop the line, and most stops being false alarms is the point
questions.why: GM's checklist culture hid problems; Toyota's empowerment culture surfaces them - the difference that survived a 15-year partnership.

questions.q: Toyota avoids cost-plus supplier pricing because:
options: A guaranteed margin breeds lethargy and kills every incentive to innovate cost out
questions.why: Relational contracts hand suppliers the design and the patents - and the incentive.

questions.q: The hold-up problem arises when:
options: One party sinks capacity against another's unverifiable forecast, then faces dictated terms
questions.why: Fixes: shared capex stakes (credible forecasts) and screening contract menus (the choice reveals private information).

questions.q: mu = 10, lambda = 9. Expected congestion L = rho/(1-rho) is:
questions.why: rho = 0.9, L = 0.9/0.1 = 9; at 95% it is 19 and at 99% it is 99 - a steep collapse, not linear degradation.

questions.q: When Mumbai airport cuts peak flights to ease congestion, the module's critique is:
options: It is killing lambda - killing sales - when the better lever is raising mu (capacity or speed)
questions.why: Too little utilisation is its own crime; the healthy zone (typically 70-90%) is set by YOUR variability, not a benchmark deck.

questions.q: On 'how much variety is right', the module's first correction was:
options: Focus is NOT about quality - quality must be complied with at any variety level; a narrow range buys cost and simplicity, not a quality badge
questions.why: And there is no analytical optimum: the call is part OS, part marketing - functional strategies are concurrent.

questions.q: Apple buying some chips from Intel (and Qualcomm) while unable to leave China buys it:
options: Tariff escape and de-risking optics - sourcing American silicon without moving the ecosystem
questions.why: Capability-wise the China-India-Vietnam ecosystem stays; the sourcing line item moves - and Intel gets a windfall.

questions.q: Amazon's post-pandemic build-out added:
options: As much fulfilment capacity in three years as in its entire first twenty-five - the map's red circles drowned in blue
questions.why: Because e-commerce differentiation moved from category to speed - and speed demands a denser, un-pooled network.

questions.q: For same-day delivery, an order must be pick-packed and ready in about:
questions.why: That number is what the blue circles - and the upward-bending cost curve - are buying.

questions.q: Amazon tweaking search to rank locally-stocked items higher is:
options: Advertising the speed it just bought - operations design surfacing in the customer interface
questions.why: The network and the algorithm are one strategy: make the fast promise, then make the fast promise visible.

questions.q: Minutes-level quick commerce 'stays an India story' because:
options: The unit economics do not survive developed-market labour costs
questions.why: Blinkit-style density prices out where riders cost ten times more - geography is an economics filter.

questions.q: Southwest ended bags-fly-free after four decades partly because:
options: Rivals' bag fees became too big an opportunity loss - and belly-heavy aircraft were choking baggage handling
questions.why: Even a signature policy is a design choice with a shelf life; the relentless turnaround focus stayed.

questions.q: Old DVD economics (wholesale ~USD 65-70, rental ~USD 3) caused:
options: Systematic under-ordering - a title had to rent twenty-plus times to break even, so hits went out of stock and customers fumed
questions.why: The revenue-sharing fix (wholesale ~10, split each rental) realigned incentives and killed the under-ordering.

questions.q: Messi's Inter Miami deal was cited as revenue sharing because he:
options: Rejected a Saudi offer at some five times the wage for a modest base plus a share of new Apple TV subscriptions and Adidas sales
questions.why: A closed-loop ecosystem contract - the DVD lesson wearing football boots.

questions.q: Netflix customers receiving requests 3,1,2,4 instead of 1,2,3,4 was:
options: The one sacrifice that let ~50 pooled warehouses aggregate demand and run allocation algorithms on shared stock
questions.why: Variety and price were the differentiators then, not speed - so pooling's lead-time cost did not bite; done expensively it would have been a 2 percent niche.

questions.q: Match the hundred-year ladder of what became variable:
options: 1910s per-piece worker output (Taylor); 1990s labour via offshoring; 2000s services (BPO, SaaS); 2020s cognition per token
questions.why: Each rung made a fixed cost variable; agentic AI just did it to managerial cognition itself.

questions.q: Klarna's numbers on the shallow end of the cognition curve:
options: About USD 0.19 a resolution, the work of some 700 full-time agents across 2.3 million conversations - roughly USD 40 million in profit improvement
questions.why: Shallow depth: AI cheaper than humans. The Microsoft-Uber zone begins past the crossover.

questions.q: Toyota handing suppliers performance characteristics instead of detailed drawings means:
options: The design, creativity and even patents belong to the supplier - relational trust replacing blueprint control
questions.why: Paired with no cost-plus pricing: a guaranteed margin breeds lethargy and kills the incentive to innovate cost out.

questions.q: Intel and Boeing made opposite sourcing errors. Their common root cause was:
options: An operations strategy misaligned with the industry's basis of competition
questions.why: Intel hoarded control in an innovation-ecosystem industry; Boeing gave away quality control in a quality industry. Fit, not level.

questions.q: DMart and IndiGo share the same left-of-matrix playbook. Its essence is:
options: Curated low variety on a standardised process, collapsing variability and cost
questions.why: Curated fast-mover assortment / single fleet type - low noise, low inventory or spares, low training cost.

questions.q: Read Zara through three module lenses. Which combination is correct?
options: Vertical integration for speed (S1); small lots trading inventory risk for shortage risk (S1); roughly twice H&M's inventory turns (S4-S5)
MTO player; high utilisation; product innovation moat
questions.why: One firm, three sessions: integration serves speed, small lots swap risk types, and Little's Law shows up as turns.

questions.q: Netflix (DVD era), Amazon (post-pandemic), FedEx (recently) and Southwest set the pooling dial at:
questions.why: Netflix pooled ~50 warehouses day one; Amazon un-pooled for speed; FedEx merged two networks; point-to-point cannot pool.

questions.q: The single principle deciding the right pooling level is:
options: Whatever your differentiation makes expensive - lead time, inventory, or shock recovery
questions.why: Pooling is a dial, not a doctrine; the differentiator prices the trade-off.

questions.q: EOQ and the newsvendor solve different trade-offs. Match them correctly:
options: EOQ: ordering cost vs cyclic holding cost; newsvendor: overage (leftover) vs underage (shortage)
EOQ: overage vs underage; newsvendor: ordering vs holding
questions.why: EOQ balances setup against carrying for repeat items; the newsvendor balances leftovers against lost profit for one-shot demand.

questions.q: Safety stock levels should primarily follow:
options: Demand/supply variability and target service level
questions.why: S3's ABC logic and S4's DMart chain agree: noise and promised service level set the buffer - volume does not.

questions.q: A firm has daily sales of Rs. 1 million and average inventory of Rs. 5 million. By Little's Law:
options: A rupee spends 5 days inside the system (turns = 1/T)
questions.why: I = R x T gives T = 5 days; turns = 1/T. The same law read Zara, DMart, Apple (~70) and Samsung (~20).

questions.q: A bank replaces three separate teller lines with one single line feeding all counters. This is:
options: Risk pooling applied to queues - one slow customer delays only one register
questions.why: The single line pools arrival variability across servers - the S5 queue example and the S4 warehouse are the same mathematics.

questions.q: Per the module's law of disruption, Netflix's DVD-by-mail qualified because it:
options: Killed the variety-vs-cost trade-off at scale via pooled warehouses and flat fees
questions.why: Unlimited variety at low cost, cheaply delivered - done expensively it would have been a 2% niche, not a disruption.

questions.q: The agentic-AI make-vs-buy principle taught in Session 5 is:
questions.why: Klarna-style task outsourcing is classic unbundling; capability transfer is the Boeing-Spirit mistake at organisational scale.

questions.q: Lemon Tree employing a large share of persons with disabilities (Session 2) worked because:
options: It was a CSR compliance rule
Effectiveness (stakeholder value) was designed first, and efficiency followed from loyal, low-attrition, high-skill staff
questions.why: Avittathur's point: design for effectiveness and efficiency often follows - the reverse rarely holds.

questions.q: Apple turns inventory ~70 times a year; Samsung ~20. The correct inference is:
options: Different diagonals of the product-process matrix - benchmark within a diagonal, never across
questions.why: Narrow curated range vs every-price-point variety: the KPI reads the business model, not the competence.

questions.q: 'High utilisation under variability is a crime' because L = rho/(1-rho) implies:
options: Congestion explodes as rho approaches 1 (rho 0.9 gives L=9; rho 0.99 gives L=99)
questions.why: The collapse is steep; a 99%-utilised system has congestion multiplier 99 - IndiGo's December arithmetic.

questions.q: Which pair are PROCESS-innovation moats rather than product moats?
options: Zara's fast supply chain and Toyota's production system
questions.why: S1's core claim: process moats are messy, cultural and durable; product moats are visible and copyable.

questions.q: The hold-up problem (Nvidia-supplier capacity game) is best solved by:
options: Shared capex stakes and screening contract menus that make private information reveal itself
questions.why: Sharing the capex makes the forecast credible; Pfizer-Biocon style menus turn contract choice into a lie detector.

questions.q: A quick-commerce dark store deliberately running riders at low utilisation illustrates:
options: Slack purchased as the product itself - speed sold as the differentiator
questions.why: S3's tyranny of utilisation: idle capacity is the cost of the 10-minute promise; the buffer IS the business model.

questions.q: China holding roughly 100 days of crude oil imports is, in Kraljic terms, managing a:
options: Strategic item with massive safety stock
questions.why: High value, high supply risk - strategic quadrant; the buffer is national-scale safety stock against disruption.

questions.q: The retailers' inventory-to-sales ratio peaking mid-recession teaches that inventory is:
options: A lagging indicator - stock piles up only after demand has already fallen
questions.why: S1's dial: by the time the pile is visible you are already deep inside the trouble.

questions.q: Boeing buying back Spirit AeroSystems and America's struggle to re-shore manufacturing both show:
options: Once a capability leaves, recovery cost is enormous - sometimes infinite; money is not the constraint
questions.why: S1's CHIPS Act lesson and S5's tasks-vs-capabilities rule are the same: lost process capability cannot simply be bought back.

questions.q: GM went bankrupt beside its own teacher (a 15-year Toyota JV) because it:
options: Copied the checklist but kept an arm's-length culture - lean parked in the OM box, never the boardroom
questions.why: Andon empowerment, relational contracts, no cost-plus - the philosophy did not transfer; culture is part of the process.

questions.q: Should a firm raise the service level for an item? The first questions to ask are:
options: What are the underage (shortage) and overage costs - and the critical ratio Cu/(Cu+Co)?
questions.why: Service level is an economic choice: the newsvendor critical ratio prices exactly how much shortage risk to tolerate.

questions.q: The one thread running through all five sessions is:
options: Every operations design must take its mandate from the differentiation strategy - misalignment is the killer
questions.why: Intel, Boeing, GM and Southwest's worst week are the same failure; Zara, Toyota, DMart and Amazon are the same success.

questions.q: Amazon un-pools; Southwest cannot pool. The key distinction is:
options: Amazon's un-pooling is a priced DECISION serving a speed differentiation; Southwest's is a structural property of point-to-point that chose which disaster it cannot absorb
questions.why: Grade the fit and the consciousness of the trade-off, never the pooling level itself.

questions.q: Klarna's USD 0.19 resolutions sit far below the human salary line. In Session 1's language, agentic AI at shallow depth has:
options: Shifted the industry frontier itself - the same service value now achievable at radically lower cost, redefining what 'on the line' means
questions.why: When technology moves the frontier, yesterday's efficient players wake up below the curve without changing anything.

questions.q: The newsvendor's 23-unit cushion, a retailer's safety stock, and China's 100 days of crude are:
options: The same logic at three scales: paying a known holding cost to escape being hostage to an uncertainty
questions.why: Safety stock is the price of the uncertainties you refuse to be hostage to - from a paowala's tray to a superpower's tanks.

questions.q: Zudio's ~47-day cover, DMart's curated fast movers and IndiGo's single fleet are one playbook:
options: Left-of-matrix designs - curate variety down, standardise the process, let low variability drive low inventory and cost leadership
questions.why: Three industries, one diagonal position - and in each case the advantage hides in a process outsiders cannot see.

questions.q: The old MDP's instant confirmations and IndiGo's short-notice rostering change share a failure mode:
options: Self-injected shocks: promising or changing before viability was confirmed, inside systems with no absorbers for the resulting variability
questions.why: If your design has no shock absorbers, your one duty is never to create the shock yourself - sequencing is a form of safety stock.

questions.q: Lemon Tree's caring design, Toyota's relational contracts and the andon cord all monetise the same asset:
options: Trust - designed into processes and contracts, it surfaces problems, retains people and converts 'extra' cost into extra revenue
questions.why: Effectiveness compounding as design: the through-line from Session 2's definition to Session 5's lean.
